newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Central Asia hails future treaty on Chinese border.
newsitem.headline: Central Asia hails future treaty on Chinese border.

text.p: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan on Tuesday hailed a treaty they will sign with Russia and China this week on reducing armed forces along the former Soviet-Chinese border as a big step towards improving security.
A spokesman for Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev said the document, due to be signed in Moscow on Thursday by the leaders of the five countries, was "historically important".

"A climate of trust among the states of the (Asian) region is being formed and legally entrenched," he said, stressing that vast oil-rich Kazakhstan shared a common border with China of around 1,700 km (1,000 miles).

"This treaty will play a great role in reinforcing security and peace in the Asian and Pacific regions," Zafar Saidov, spokesman for Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, said by telephone from the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
Sergei Dedyukhin, spokesman to Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev said "the document lays the ground for the (Asian) region's stability in the 21st century".

Not all the details of the treaty, first negotiated in May 1990 when Russia and the Central Asian states of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan were republics within the former Soviet Union, have yet been made public.
But, unveiling some of them, the spokesman for the Kazakh leader said the military forces of the five states deployed near the border would be reduced and pulled back 100 km (60 miles).
He said the five countries would regularly exchange information regarding the situation on their parts of the border and allow mutual inspections to monitor armed forces reductions.
"This will provide for a larger degree of transparency in relations among the five states," he said.
But while it eases security along the Chinese border, Thursday's treaty is unlikely to lessen tension in other parts of Central Asia.
Around 20,000 Russian troops will remain in Tajikistan, guarding its border with Afghanistan and seeing themselves as a shield against the possible spread of militant Islam.

The ceasefire reached in December between Tajikistan's secular government and the country's Islamist opposition ended a four-year civil war but the peace is often disturbed by fighters of unknown loyalties who operate from bases in Afghanistan.
Cheap Afghan opium and its derivatives have flooded narcotics markets in Central Asia.

Russia's recent decision to place units of armed Cossacks -- a warrior class of ethnic Russians which spearheaded Russian expansion in Tsarist times -- along its nearly 5,000 km (3,100 miles) border with Kazakhstan is another source of tension.
Kazakhstan's foreign ministry last week expressed its "serious concern" about the deployment of the Russian Cossacks along the Kazakh border.
Russia said its Cossack patrols were not armed but in the future they might be given weapons to fight "irregularities, mostly in drugs and smuggling".
